ed.name: Madagascar
ed.stripDate: Referendum planned May–July 2027, presidential election September–December 2027 (dates not yet fixed)
facts: 5 (transition, former ruling coalition, two opposition parties, Gen Z)
system: Protests led by young people (“Gen Z”) began on 25 September 2025 over water and power cuts; the UN counted at least 22 deaths in the first days. On 12–13 October soldiers of the CAPSAT unit joined the protesters, President Andry Rajoelina left the country, and the National Assembly impeached him on 14 October. The High Constitutional Court (HCC) entrusted CAPSAT commander Colonel Michaël Randrianirina with the duties of head of state; he was sworn in on 17 October 2025 as “President of the Refondation of the Republic”. The African Union suspended Madagascar.

The Refondation programme sent to SADC in February 2026 has four stages: a national consultation, new electoral rules and a new voter roll, a constitution for a Fifth Republic approved by referendum (or a “constitutional election”) in May–July 2027, then a presidential election in September–December 2027. In May 2026 the electoral commission (CENI) proposed June and October 2027; in August the head of state spoke of a first vote in July 2027. In October 2026 he called elections in 2027 his “dearest wish”, but no decree has fixed the dates.
How the next president will be elected

The 2010 constitution is suspended. The voting system, term and candidacy conditions for 2027 depend on the new constitution and electoral laws still being drafted. The national consultation, entrusted to the churches’ council (FFKM), runs from the fokontany (neighbourhood) level upwards, and its conclusions are not expected before May 2027; the Presidency also consulted more than 80 parties in September 2026.
Who can vote and who runs the vote
The CENI is rebuilding the voter roll from scratch, with a registration committee in each neighbourhood. Registration began on 28 July 2026 and should end between April and June 2027.

Rajoelina lives in exile, mostly in Dubai; a decree of 24 October 2025 ended his Malagasy nationality because he had acquired French nationality, and a judge is investigating the certificate he used to run in 2023. Most MPs elected for his IRMAR coalition have rallied to the new authorities. Opposition parties such as Marc Ravalomanana’s TIM and the HVM take part in the consultations; few have named candidates or published programmes, and Colonel Randrianirina has not said whether he will run.

The authorities say they guarantee freedom of expression, but in April 2026 several Gen Z activists were arrested after peaceful protests and two were charged with undermining state security; Amnesty International called for their release. In October 2026 seven political groupings said the Refondation was drifting and warned against a hasty election that would only change the people in office.
ed.status: Positions in this edition were coded from the transition authorities’ decisions, budgets and statements, the record of former President Rajoelina’s government, and statements by IRMAR, TIM, HVM and Gen Z activists published up to 16 October 2026. They have not yet been validated by the parties or by an independent committee. This is not an ordinary campaign: the vote will be organised by a military-led transition, its dates and rules are not fixed, no party has published a programme and few have named candidates, so many positions come from records or isolated statements and several cells are missing. The transition authorities are not a party and Colonel Randrianirina has not said whether he will run; Gen Z is a protest movement, not a registered party.
others: Seven groupings critical of the Refondation (Vovonana Loharano, Vato Nasondrotra ny Tany, Vondrona Ampandrana, HPM, G5, Tafita, Dimbin’Iarivo)
Firaisankina, Tsy Manaiky Lembenana, Mouvement Gasikara, KFim, Siap

questions.text: Madagascar should adopt its new constitution before electing a president.
questions.ctx: The Refondation programme plans a new constitution approved by referendum or a “constitutional election” in May–July 2027, then a presidential election in September–December 2027. Technicians say the timetable is tight, and the reverse option has been discussed: elect a president first and let them organise the referendum. Supporters of the first order say the rules must exist before anyone is elected; critics fear a longer transition.

mg_ref.n: The Refondation programme (February 2026) puts the constitutional vote before the presidential one, but says its deadlines can be revised; holding the presidential vote first was discussed behind the scenes in August 2026.

mg_hvm.n: HVM president Rivo Rakotovao (September 2026): “Il faut d’abord examiner la question de la Constitution avant la tenue de l’élection présidentielle.”

nd.mg_tim: TIM asks for a clear calendar and for the December 2027 date to be kept, but this edition found no TIM statement on which vote should come first.
nd.mg_irmar: No IRMAR statement found on the order of the votes.

questions.text: The national consultation led by the churches’ council (FFKM) is the right way to prepare the new constitution.
questions.ctx: The transition entrusted a nationwide consultation, from the fokontany up to national level, to the FFKM (Council of Christian Churches); its conclusions are expected after May 2027 and should shape the new constitution. Supporters say the churches are trusted mediators in past crises; critics say the process is slow and vague and want a body set up for the purpose.

mg_ref.n: In August 2026 Colonel Randrianirina confirmed that the national consultation is entrusted to the FFKM, from the local level up to the national level.

mg_tim.n: Ravalomanana (April 2026) said TIM will take an active part, because the process “va définir le système de gouvernance du pays et les règles du jeu des élections”.

mg_hvm.n: HVM says it will take part in the Refondation and is consulting its members to bring a common position to the national consultation (September 2026).

mg_irmar.n: IRMAR’s parliamentary leader Philobert Milavonjy said in March 2026 that the coalition will take “full” part in the national consultation, even without Rajoelina.

mg_genz.n: Gen Z marchers (April 2026) asked what the consultation is really for and called for a “pré-concertation” to set up its bodies, including a constituent assembly.

questions.text: The new constitution should be written by a constituent assembly set up for that purpose.
questions.ctx: Critics say the 2010 constitution was drafted by a narrow circle, without a constituent assembly. Under the current plan, the FFKM-led consultation produces proposals and a constituent assembly would only be set up if the consultation recommends one. Supporters say an assembly would give citizens ownership of the text; others fear more delay before elections.

mg_genz.n: Gen Z marchers (April 2026) called for bodies including a constituent assembly and a people’s committee at fokonolona (community) level.

mg_ref.n: The transition’s plan leaves this open: a constituent assembly is mentioned only as a possibility if the national consultation recommends one (August 2026).

questions.text: Parties close to former President Rajoelina should take full part in the national dialogue on the country’s future.
questions.ctx: After the October 2025 takeover, several of Rajoelina’s former ministers and allies left the country, were arrested or are under investigation. His IRMAR coalition says it wants to take part in the national consultation, and the Presidency invited an IRMAR group to its September 2026 talks. Supporters say a lasting settlement must include every camp; critics say those accused of corruption should not shape the new rules.

mg_ref.n: The Presidency’s September 2026 consultations at Iavoloha included an IRMAR group among more than 80 parties.

mg_irmar.n: IRMAR (March 2026) said it is ready to bring proposals, to join all debates aimed at stability, and called for everyone to be involved.

mg_hvm.n: HVM calls on all political forces to talk to each other: “Il faut avoir le courage de se parler et d’échanger sur le développement du pays.”

questions.text: The High Constitutional Court (HCC) should be replaced by a new Constitutional Council.
questions.ctx: In October 2025 the HCC handed the duties of head of state to Colonel Randrianirina, a decision some jurists say legalised a coup; in 2023 it had validated Rajoelina’s candidacy. In July 2026 the head of state discussed the creation of a Constitutional Council with former Presidents Ravalomanana and Rajaonarimampianina; no decision was taken.

mg_ref.n: The Presidency (July 2026): “Madagascar a besoin d’un Conseil constitutionnel pour valider les lois et arbitrer les crises.”

mg_tim.n: TIM says such a Council must guarantee “le respect du vote et un calendrier électoral clair” (July 2026).

mg_hvm.n: HVM wants an independent, legally solid body “qui sécurise la transition sans la paralyser” (July 2026).

mg_genz.n: Gen Z marchers demanded the dissolution of the HCC in April 2026; in October 2025 they had already called for its “refondation”.

questions.text: The National Assembly elected in 2024 should be dissolved before the end of the transition.
questions.ctx: The military kept the National Assembly when it took power; the Assembly impeached Rajoelina on 14 October 2025 and has since examined the transition’s budgets. Most MPs elected for Rajoelina’s IRMAR coalition have rallied to the new authorities. Gen Z activists accuse MPs of switching sides and of failing to check the government.

mg_genz.n: Gen Z marchers (April 2026) demanded the dissolution of the National Assembly, criticising MPs’ “versatilité”.

mg_ref.n: The military kept the National Assembly in place when it took power in October 2025, and it still sits.

nd.mg_irmar: IRMAR leads the opposition group in the Assembly; this edition found no statement from it on dissolution.

questions.text: The electoral commission (CENI) should be dissolved and rebuilt before the next votes.
questions.ctx: The CENI was set up under the previous regime and organised the 2023 presidential election. The transition kept it: in May 2026 it announced it would erase the voter roll and rebuild it from scratch. Gen Z activists want it dissolved; the authorities say it should regain public trust through transparent methods.

mg_genz.n: Gen Z marchers (April 2026) demanded the dissolution of the CENI along with the National Assembly and the HCC.

mg_ref.n: The transition kept the CENI; in August 2026 Colonel Randrianirina said he supports its consultations on electoral governance and expects it to be ready from July 2027.

questions.text: The new constitution should abolish the Senate.
questions.ctx: Under the 2010 constitution, part of the Senate was elected indirectly and part appointed by the president. During the October 2025 protests Gen Z activists demanded its “dissolution totale”, or at least the departure of its president, General Richard Ravalomanana, who was replaced by the senators on 12 October 2025. The new constitution will decide whether Madagascar keeps a second chamber.

mg_genz.n: Gen Z’s written demands (October 2025) included the “dissolution totale du Sénat”, or at minimum the departure of its president.

nd.mg_ref: This edition found no statement by the transition authorities on the Senate’s future in the new constitution.

questions.text: The presidential election must take place by December 2027 at the latest.
questions.ctx: The international community endorsed a transition of about 24 months, and SADC called in August 2026 for a “return to constitutional normalcy”. The CENI proposed October 2027 for the presidential vote; the Refondation programme says September–December 2027 and calls its dates revisable. Seven political groupings warn that a rushed vote would only change the people in office.

mg_ref.n: Randrianirina (October 2026) said holding the elections in 2027 is his “souhait le plus cher” and that he is “un homme de parole”.

mg_tim.n: TIM’s secretary-general (March 2026): “Nous espérons que l’annonce de l’organisation de l’élection en décembre 2027 sera maintenue.”

nd.mg_hvm: HVM wants the constitution settled first and the presidential vote last, but did not oppose a 2027 date.

questions.text: The voter roll should be rebuilt from scratch, even if this takes time.
questions.ctx: In May 2026 the CENI announced it would erase existing voter databases and rebuild the roll within eleven months, with a registration committee in each neighbourhood open to parties and civil society. Registration began on 28 July 2026 and should end between April and June 2027. Distrust of the roll has fuelled disputes over past elections.

mg_ref.n: The CENI is erasing the old databases and rebuilding the roll from the smallest administrative units: “Nous allons utiliser des modes opératoires vraiment transparents.”

mg_tim.n: TIM (March 2026): “La révision et le nettoyage de la liste électorale, gages de la confiance du peuple, n’ont pas encore donné de résultats.”

mg_hvm.n: HVM wants electoral reform for more transparent elections and restored trust, starting from the fokontany level (September 2026).

questions.text: Anyone who has voluntarily taken another country’s nationality should be barred from running for president.
questions.ctx: A decree of 24 October 2025 ended Andry Rajoelina’s Malagasy nationality because he had voluntarily acquired French nationality, and in September 2026 a judge opened an investigation into the nationality certificate he used to run in 2023. The HCC had validated that candidacy in 2023, ruling that the certificate was valid until proven otherwise. The rule will shape who can run in 2027.

mg_ref.n: The transition ended Rajoelina’s nationality by decree (24 October 2025); a complaint from the Prime Minister’s legal department led to a judicial investigation in September 2026.

mg_tim.n: Ravalomanana (April 2025) said the HCC kept Rajoelina’s 2023 candidacy against the Constitution and that his movement did not want to run against “un candidat vazaha, étranger”.

mg_irmar.n: Rajoelina ran and won in 2023 with a nationality certificate obtained after he had acquired French nationality; the HCC validated his candidacy.

questions.text: Military officers who took power in October 2025 should not run in the 2027 presidential election.
questions.ctx: Colonel Randrianirina has toured the regions but has no party base and has not said whether he will run. In other transitions in Africa, military leaders have run in the elections that ended the transition, which critics say undermines a level playing field; supporters say voters should be free to choose.

mg_ref.n: Randrianirina (December 2025): “Right now, I am working, and I am not thinking about being a candidate at this time” — he has not ruled out running.

nd.mg_tim: No TIM statement found on military candidates.

questions.text: Former President Andry Rajoelina should be tried in Madagascar.
questions.ctx: Rajoelina left on a French military aircraft in October 2025 and lives mostly in exile. The new authorities accuse him of plundering public resources; the Court of Accounts documented diversions of public money to his inner circle, but he has not been prosecuted so far. His allies call the cases against former regime figures political revenge.

mg_ref.n: Randrianirina (December 2025): “Our wish is to try him in Madagascar,” accusing him of impoverishing the nation.

mg_genz.n: Analysts describe convictions of former regime officials as the movement’s main demand (November 2025); this edition found no Gen Z statement on Rajoelina’s own trial.

mg_irmar.n: IRMAR’s parliamentary leader called the prosecution of a former Rajoelina minister a “chasse aux sorcières” and “vengeance politique” (January 2026); no statement found on Rajoelina’s own case.

questions.text: Former ministers and MPs of the old regime who are under investigation should lose their immunity and face the courts.
questions.ctx: In January 2026, at the request of the judicial authorities, the National Assembly’s bureau lifted the immunity of MP Marie-Michelle Sahondrarimalala, a former education minister under Rajoelina, so she could be investigated; she is banned from leaving the country. Rajoelina’s close associate Mamy Ravatomanga has been detained in Mauritius since October 2025 in a financial-crimes case; his wife calls it a “political elimination”.

mg_ref.n: The immunity was lifted at the request of the judicial authorities so they could investigate “plusieurs affaires de violation de la loi” (January 2026).

mg_irmar.n: Philobert Milavonjy, head of IRMAR’s group, called it a “chasse aux sorcières” and “vengeance politique” (January 2026); in March 2026 he again asked the government to stop persecuting IRMAR members.

mg_genz.n: Convictions of former regime officials are described as the movement’s main demand (November 2025).

questions.text: People who organise peaceful protests should not be prosecuted for “undermining state security”.
questions.ctx: In April 2026 police arrested four Gen Z members after a peaceful protest of about 100 people against power cuts, water cuts and corruption; two others were charged with “atteinte à la sûreté de l’État” for planning a new protest. Amnesty International called for their immediate release. The head of state said politicians and foreign money were behind the protests.

mg_genz.n: Gen Z leader Herizo Andriamanantena: “Nous avons manifesté contre le délestage, les coupures d’eau et la corruption généralisée.” The movement wants its members freed.

mg_ref.n: Under the transition, the organisers were arrested and two were charged with undermining state security and disturbing public order (April 2026).

nd.mg_tim: TIM said in March 2026 that freedom of expression and movement had improved; no statement found on the April arrests.

questions.text: Fighting corruption should be the transition’s first priority.
questions.ctx: Corruption was a core grievance of the 2025 protests, alongside water and power cuts. The first Council of Ministers in October 2025 set six priorities (energy, water, health, education, youth jobs and support for reform) and stressed the fight against corruption. Civil-society groups ask ministers to publish their asset declarations.

mg_genz.n: The fight against corruption is described as “la revendication principale” of the movement (November 2025).

mg_ref.n: The first Council of Ministers (October 2025) stressed the fight against corruption, but listed energy and water as its first two priorities.

questions.text: Electricity and water should get more public money than any other sector, including health and education.
questions.ctx: The 2025 uprising began over chronic water and power cuts. The 2026 budget gives 646 billion ariary to energy (JIRAMA’s recovery and renewables) and 140 billion to water, against 89 billion for health and 75 billion for primary and secondary schools. The power shortfall on the Antananarivo grid roughly halved between September 2025 and September 2026, but cuts continue.

mg_ref.n: The 2026 budget makes energy and water its priorities, with 646 billion and 140 billion ariary.

mg_genz.n: Gen Z activist Mihary Rakotondravelo (September 2026), on persistent water and power cuts: “The basic demands still haven’t been met.”

mg_tim.n: TIM (March 2026): “L’important pour le peuple reste la santé et l’éducation.”

questions.text: Contracts with private power producers that no longer suit the country should be renegotiated or cancelled.
questions.ctx: JIRAMA, the state water and power utility, relies on private producers and rented generators and owes them and fuel suppliers about 1,493 billion ariary under its recovery-plan baseline. Supporters of a review say some contracts drain JIRAMA; producers say they need clear terms and to be paid.

mg_ref.n: JIRAMA’s director general, General Hajatiana Rasolomanana (August 2026): “Les contrats qui ne sont plus en adéquation avec les réalités actuelles seront examinés.”

nd.mg_irmar: The contracts were largely signed under Rajoelina’s government; this edition found no IRMAR statement on reviewing them.

questions.text: The state should keep covering JIRAMA’s losses rather than raise electricity prices.
questions.ctx: JIRAMA produces electricity at about 1,225 ariary per kWh and sells it at about 795, a loss of roughly 1,030 billion ariary a year, and depends on state support. In 2025 Rajoelina’s government planned tariff rises and staff cuts in a recovery plan the IMF required. Higher prices would cut losses but hit households and firms, for which power is already a heavy cost.

mg_ref.n: The transition authorised the state procurement company to import diesel for JIRAMA, which still relies on state support; no tariff increase had been announced by October 2026.

mg_irmar.n: Rajoelina’s ministers presented a JIRAMA recovery plan including “une hausse des tarifs pour réduire les pertes d’exploitation” and fewer staff (June 2025).

questions.text: Large dams such as Volobe and Sahofika should be the main answer to power cuts, even if they take years to build.
questions.ctx: Antananarivo’s grid depends on hydropower and costly diesel plants. JIRAMA’s plan relies on solar power (52 MW installed), large hydro projects (Volobe, Sahofika, Antetezambato) and new power lines; meanwhile the state is buying or renting generators from Russia, China and South Africa. Business groups say generators only solve part of the problem.

mg_ref.n: The transition’s energy plan relies on large hydro projects (Volobe, Sahofika, Antetezambato), solar and transmission lines, with generators as a stopgap (October 2026).

mg_irmar.n: Rajoelina’s government said its hydroelectric projects to raise output were validated under the IMF programme (June 2025).

questions.text: Madagascar should keep its IMF programme, even with conditions such as automatic fuel-price adjustment and a JIRAMA recovery plan.
questions.ctx: Madagascar has an IMF Extended Credit Facility and a Resilience and Sustainability Facility. In 2025 the IMF asked for a decree on automatic fuel-price adjustment, a revised budget and a clear JIRAMA recovery plan. On 30 September 2026 the IMF board approved the third and fourth reviews, unlocking about US$155 million. Supporters say the programme brings cheap financing; critics say its conditions can push up prices.

mg_ref.n: The transition kept the programme; the IMF approved its third and fourth reviews on 30 September 2026, and the Finance Ministry is preparing the 2027 budget with the IMF.

mg_irmar.n: Rajoelina’s government ran the programme and worked on its 2025 conditions, including the fuel-price decree and the JIRAMA plan.

questions.text: The state should cut its running costs to spend more on investment such as roads and power.
questions.ctx: The 2026 budget, called a budget of “sobriété”, aims to lower current spending over time in favour of investment, with 440 billion ariary for roads. It also raises civil-service salaries and pensions and creates thousands of teaching posts. Critics of austerity say public services are already underfunded.

mg_ref.n: The 2026 budget sets “un objectif de baisse tendancielle des charges courantes au profit de l’investissement”.

questions.text: Madagascar should finance its budget mainly by collecting more taxes and customs duties, rather than by borrowing abroad.
questions.ctx: The 2026 budget aims to raise tax revenue to 6,221.7 billion ariary, up from about 5,101 billion expected in 2025, with tighter customs controls; VAT is the largest source. The deficit is still financed mainly by external loans and budget support. Higher collection would reduce debt, but businesses and consumers fear a heavier burden.

mg_ref.n: The 2026 budget raises the tax target sharply and tightens customs controls, but still relies mainly on external borrowing and budget support for the deficit.

questions.text: The state should recruit thousands of new teachers every year, even if the public wage bill grows.
questions.ctx: The 2026 budget creates 9,000 teaching posts in primary and secondary schools and 100 university posts. Many schools rely on teachers paid by parents’ associations. Supporters say more teachers are the fastest way to improve learning; critics worry about the wage bill.

mg_ref.n: The 2026 budget creates 9,000 teaching posts and 100 university posts.

mg_tim.n: TIM (March 2026) says health and education are what matter most to the people.

mg_genz.n: Young protesters want better teaching conditions and jobs after their studies (November 2025).

questions.text: The state should hire more health workers and raise their allowances, even if other spending must be cut.
questions.ctx: The 2026 budget gives 89 billion ariary to health, with 500 new posts and higher risk allowances. Regions such as Atsimo Andrefana lack specialist doctors. Supporters say health is a basic right; others say the budget must first fix power and water.

mg_ref.n: The 2026 budget creates 500 health posts and raises risk allowances, but gives far more to energy.

mg_tim.n: TIM (March 2026): “L’important pour le peuple reste la santé et l’éducation.”

questions.short: Youth jobs as a top priority
questions.text: Creating jobs for young people should be one of the state’s top budget priorities.
questions.ctx: Youth unemployment and underemployment fed the 2025 protests. The transition listed job creation for young people among its six priorities and asked each ministry to set up a platform for young people. Critics say no large-scale jobs programme has been announced.

mg_ref.n: Job creation for young people is one of the six priorities set by the first Council of Ministers (October 2025).

mg_genz.n: Young protesters want jobs after their studies (November 2025).

questions.text: Gen Z representatives should be appointed to the government and to the bodies running the transition.
questions.ctx: Gen Z activists sit on the national consultation committees, but none of the candidates they proposed joined the government formed in March 2026, which kept most former ministers. The head of state told young protesters to “learn real politics”. Supporters say the movement earned a seat at the table; others say ministers should be chosen for competence, not for activism.

mg_genz.n: Herizo Andriamanantena (March 2026): Gen Z put forward candidates, none was even interviewed, and young people feel they “n’ont pas leur mot à dire”.

mg_ref.n: The government formed on 25 March 2026 kept most former ministers and included none of the Gen Z candidates.

questions.short: Work with SADC on the timetable
questions.text: Madagascar should agree its transition timetable with the Southern African Development Community (SADC).
questions.ctx: The African Union suspended Madagascar after the takeover. The transition sent its Refondation programme to SADC in February 2026, and in August 2026 Colonel Randrianirina discussed the electoral calendar with South Africa’s President Ramaphosa at the SADC summit, which called for a return to constitutional normalcy. SADC envoys also met IRMAR in March 2026 and said they would not impose solutions.

mg_ref.n: The transition submitted its Refondation programme to SADC and announced its election calendar after talks with Ramaphosa at the SADC summit (August 2026).

mg_irmar.n: IRMAR met SADC envoys in March 2026 to discuss the crisis.

questions.text: Madagascar should tie its development more closely to its southern African neighbours.
questions.ctx: Madagascar is a member of SADC and of the Indian Ocean Commission, and France remains a major partner. Since 2025 the authorities have relaunched cooperation with countries such as Botswana. Supporters of closer regional integration see new markets; others say the island’s main trade and aid partners are elsewhere.

mg_tim.n: Ravalomanana (July 2026) called for greater openness to southern African countries, saying development depends on regional cooperation: “La confiance mutuelle est le fondement du développement.”

nd.mg_ref: The transition works closely with SADC on its timetable, but this edition found no statement on regional economic integration.

questions.text: Madagascar should seek help from Russia as well as from Western partners such as France.
questions.ctx: France evacuated Rajoelina in October 2025 and remains a key partner; the transition accepted French support after a call with President Macron. The National Assembly’s president visited Moscow, and in 2026 the state ordered 18 emergency generators from Russia. Supporters say diversifying partners brings more help; critics fear new dependencies.

mg_ref.n: Asked about the Assembly president’s trip to Moscow, Randrianirina said “We are open to all types of collaboration”; he also accepted French support (December 2025).
